label: Power, battery, sound
rationale: Switching a device on and off, and the times it stops working: a dead battery or no sound.
mixUps: dengen o ireru / kiru (you switch it on or off) vs juuden ga kireru (it runs out on its own) is transitive kiru vs intransitive kireru, as in denwa o kiru / denwa ga kireta. Lights and the TV take tsukeru / kesu, and oto ga deru (sound comes out of a device) is not oto ga suru (you hear a noise).

targets.verbSense: cut; cut off (a call, the power)
targets.trap: Not sumaho o kesu: powering a phone or device down is dengen o kiru ('cut the power'), with the device joined by no (sumaho no dengen kitte), or casually just keitai kitte; dengen o otosu is common too. Sumaho kesu can sound like turning only the screen off; kesu is for lights and the TV, though pasokon kesu is heard.
targets.use: Said about switching off a phone or other device, as an excuse (gomen, dengen kitteta = sorry, my phone was off) or a fix (ikkai dengen kitte mite). Cinema and exam announcements say keitai denwa no dengen o okiri kudasai. Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: On is dengen o ireru, and a phone that won't start is dengen ga hairanai (or tsukanai); one that shuts itself off is dengen kireta. Shutting down a computer is often dengen o otosu (pasokon otoshita). The kiru is the one in denwa o kiru.

example.english: Try turning it off for a moment.

examplePolite.romaji: ichido dengen o kitte mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 一度電源を切ってみてください。
examplePolite.english: Please try turning it off for a moment.

targets.verbSense: put in; switch on (the power, a switch)
targets.trap: English 'turn on' pulls toward tsukeru, the verb for the appliance itself (denki, terebi, eakon). The power or a switch usually takes ireru ('put in'); dengen tsukeru is heard, but much less. Join the device with no: sumaho no dengen irete.
partners: eakon (air conditioner; tsukeru is more usual)
targets.use: Said about switching on a phone, computer or machine, often while troubleshooting: dengen ireta? (did you turn it on?). A device that won't start is dengen ga hairanai (or tsukanai), with intransitive hairu. Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: Off is dengen o kiru. For a computer, pasokon tsukeru and kidou suru (boot up) are heard too.

example.english: Did you actually turn it on?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, purojekutaa no dengen o irete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、プロジェクターの電源を入れてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you turn on the projector?

targets.verbSense: be cut; run out (of a supply, charge or time)
targets.trap: Not shinu: a dead phone is juuden kireta ('the charge ran out'). denchi kireta, juuden nakunatta and batterii kireta are also fine; sumaho shinda is slang.
targets.use: Said when a phone dies, in the past: juuden kireta / kirechatta (my phone died). About to die is juuden kiresou (or juuden yabai, slangy); low but not dead is juuden ga nai.
targets.notes: Charging is the plain verb juuden suru. The same kireru is a dropped call: denwa kireta (the call cut off). Switching the phone off yourself is dengen o kiru, the transitive half.

example.ja: ごめん、充電切れちゃった。

examplePolite.ja: すみません、充電が切れちゃいました。

targets.english: sound comes out (of a TV, speaker, phone)
targets.trap: Not oto ga ugokanai: when a TV, speaker or call goes silent, the sound 'doesn't come out', oto ga denai. oto nai is heard too, and it is the plain way to say a clip has no sound at all: kono douga, oto nai yo.
targets.use: Said about TVs, speakers, laptops and video calls, most often in the negative or as a check: oto denai (there's no sound), oto deteru? (is there sound?). ga is usually dropped, and on a call oto dete nai yo means your sound isn't coming through.
targets.notes: Different from oto ga suru (you hear a noise). Muting is oto o kesu; turning it down is oto o sageru.

example.romaji: are, oto denai n da kedo.
example.ja: あれ、音出ないんだけど。

examplePolite.romaji: are, oto ga denai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、音が出ないんですけど。

reviewPool.english: be hooked on games; be really into games
get lost (wander off, like a lost child)
